item.title: Pregnancy is the ‘perfect storm’ for eating disorders, but doctors keep missing them
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, clear detail

Reporting for this story was supported by the Pulitzer Center.

— Katye Jorgensen had been fighting anorexia and bulimia for years when she got pregnant at 25. Weigh-ins at prenatal appointments filled her with dread and certain foods terrified her, but she powered through for her baby’s sake. Then she struggled to breastfeed her son and lose weight after giving birth, and her mental health deteriorated.

After her second pregnancy two years later, Jorgensen became obsessive about exercise and fixated on comments about how well she was “bouncing back.” At her husband’s urging, she started seeing a therapist and a dietitian. Eventually, they staged an intervention and she agreed to enter intensive treatment, which she said saved her life.

“I went to my postpartum appointment, I mentioned a lot of this, and even though I really liked those doctors, it still didn’t set off any red alarms for anybody,” said Jorgensen, who is now 37.

Jorgensen is one of many women who struggle with eating disorders before and after childbirth but slip through the cracks of the U.S. health care system. Research suggests about 4.3% of pregnant women and more than 9% of new mothers experience eating disorders such as anorexia nervosa, bulimia nervosa, or binge eating disorder, though research is limited and no one knows their exact toll.

Those rates are on par with national averages: an estimated 2.6% to 8.4% of women will experience an eating disorder over their lifetimes — that’s up to 14.6 million women and girls in the United States.

Eating disorders have been linked to health issues for pregnant women — including miscarriage, high blood pressure, anemia, and bleeding — and complications for their developing babies, including small head circumference, low birthweight, autism, and asthma. After birth, women with a history of eating disorders appear more likely to experience postpartum depression and anxiety and to report problems feeding their newborns.

The risks vary by eating disorder. Studies don’t prove that eating disorders directly cause these issues and not everyone with a perinatal eating disorder will experience them. Still, the evidence is enough to worry clinicians.

“If we don’t treat these disorders … there are risks involved there. This isn’t a neutral situation,” said Leah Graves, a registered dietitian and a clinical adviser at the National Eating Disorders Association.

Few screening tools have been validated for eating disorders in pregnancy, and none are widely used. Obstetricians typically receive very little training about these conditions, leaving them unequipped to identify or manage eating disorders. And even with a diagnosis, many pregnant women and new mothers don’t receive timely treatment due to spotty insurance coverage and a shortage of local specialists, according to research and interviews with more than a dozen eating disorder researchers, doctors, dietitians, therapists, policy advocates, and mothers.

“It’s been a huge gap,” said Elizabeth Claydon, an associate professor at West Virginia University who researches eating disorders. “People have had this; they’ve lived with eating disorders during pregnancy. We just haven’t caught them and been able to help.”

Why is this a high-risk period?

Eating disorders usually develop in adolescence or young adulthood, but they can also emerge around pregnancy, menopause, or other periods of profound physical and life change.

Several factors can raise the risks in pregnancy: the feeling of a lack of control, rapid physical and hormonal changes, negative body image, scrutiny of the pregnant person’s diet and weight for medical reasons, the need to consume extra calories to breastfeed, a new identity and family role, and societal pressure to return to pre-pregnancy weight and succeed at motherhood.

Many women struggle with body image issues or unhealthy thoughts or behaviors around food, weight, or exercise that don’t meet the criteria for a clinical diagnosis. Pregnancy can tip the scales into an active eating disorder.

Pregnancy can also hide symptoms that overlap with eating disorders, such as nausea, vomiting, appetite changes or pumping breast milk specifically to burn calories, said Christine Call, an assistant professor of psychiatry at the University of Pittsburgh.

But many women hide their symptoms, making it difficult for doctors, or even family members, to know when someone needs help.

There’s no single trajectory in the perinatal period. Some women with eating disorders fare better during pregnancy and sustain that recovery, while others relapse once their child is born. Other women, years into recovery, see their eating disorders come roaring back in pregnancy or postpartum. Some struggle throughout pregnancy, with no respite. And others develop an eating disorder for the first time in the perinatal period.

“There’s so much shame and guilt about eating and doing things right, taking care of yourself for your baby during this period,” Call said.

Jennifer Kreatsoulas was diagnosed with anorexia 15 years before her first pregnancy, but her eating disorder “came back with a vengeance” after her second child was born, alongside postpartum depression. She decided to seek treatment when she realized she was too weak to push a stroller while out on a Mother’s Day walk with her husband and 1-year-old daughter.

“It’s destructive, but I was really trying to cope, and my brain just switched back to what it knew how to do from all those years previous,” said Kreatsoulas, now 50 and living in Pennsylvania. She attributes her relapse to “hormones, lack of sleep, complete overwhelm, your identity becoming something that you don’t know — you lose yourself in it, just because that’s what’s demanded as a mother.”

Screening and identification gaps…

item.title: mRNA Ebola vaccine trial starts in Uganda: Institute
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, clear detail

mRNA Ebola vaccine trial starts in Uganda: Institute

Trials of an experimental Ebola vaccine aimed at the strain behind the current outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo have begun in neighboring Uganda, its virus research institute said Friday.

There are currently no vaccines or treatments for the less common Bundibugyo strain of Ebola behind the outbreak in DRC, which has led to more than 5,700 confirmed deaths out of more than 11,000 cases since being declared in May, according to the World Health Organization (WHO).

Two experimental vaccines are due to start testing on Monday in the outbreak's epicenter in eastern DRC, focusing on contacts of cases and people deemed at high risk of infection.

But neighboring Uganda announced it had also launched a trial of one of the vaccines, developed by the U.S.-based Moderna group using the mRNA technology made famous during the COVID pandemic.

The Uganda Virus Research Institute said in a statement it had "launched Africa's first mRNA phase 1 clinical trial ... in collaboration with Moderna of an investigational vaccine against Bundibugyo ebolavirus."

The trial is aimed at testing the vaccine in a group of 224 healthy volunteers aged between 1 and 65 to measure its safety and immunity potential.

Despite a long and porous border with eastern DRC, Uganda has successfully contained the virus after receiving some imported cases earlier this year.

It was declared Ebola-free in August after registering 20 cases, including two deaths.

item.title: In a first, ultrasound maps blood flow through an entire human kidney in 3D
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, clear detail

In a first, ultrasound maps blood flow through an entire human kidney in 3D

For the first time, a research team at the Inserm Institute of Physics for Medicine (Inserm/ESPCI Paris-PSL/CNRS) in Paris has succeeded in visualizing the entire vascular network and blood flow in a human kidney. This breakthrough opens up promising clinical prospects: improving our understanding and diagnosis of kidney diseases linked to vascular defects. To achieve this, the researchers used a new ultrasound technique developed in their laboratory and previously tested in animals, which could eventually be extended to other organs. The results are published in The Lancet Medical Imaging & Theranostics.

The proper functioning of an organ depends closely on its vascular network. When arteries or veins are abnormal, the cells' needs for oxygen and nutrients are not met as effectively, and cellular waste is not eliminated as efficiently. The organs then suffer.

The kidney is particularly affected: changes in its microvasculature play a major role in many kidney diseases. This is particularly true of hypertensive nephrosclerosis and diabetic nephropathy, which are characterized by progressive damage to the small arteries and arterioles of the kidney, contributing to the loss of its filtration function.

"Currently, there is no specific biomarker that can directly detect these vascular abnormalities and monitor their progression. And the imaging techniques currently used cannot visualize the affected arterioles, whether it be conventional ultrasound—which lacks sufficient resolution—or MRI and CT scans," explains Clément Papadacci, an Inserm research fellow and team leader at the Institute of Physics for Medicine (Inserm/ESPCI Paris-PSL/CNRS).

Consequently, in the absence of early diagnosis and intervention, the disease is a major contributor to the development of kidney failure, requiring patients to undergo dialysis.

Directly observing the small blood vessels involved in kidney diseases is therefore a major challenge for clinicians. It is for this purpose, among others, that the team has developed a new ultrasound technique in recent years. By combining several innovations, they have developed an ultrasound probe that makes it possible to visualize the entire vascular system of an organ in three dimensions—down to the smallest capillaries—and to track blood flow in real time.

This is a remarkable achievement, given that some vessels are 50 micrometers in diameter—the size of a fine hair—and that conventional ultrasound can only visualize vessels 1 to 2 millimeters in diameter, or the size of the head of a pin.

The team has already demonstrated the effectiveness of this tool in animals for visualizing the vascular system of kidneys—and even entire hearts and livers. Now, they have demonstrated its feasibility in humans.

For the first time, the team is providing images of entire kidneys along with quantitative data on the organ's complete vascular architecture—from the largest arteries down to the microvessels—and the blood flow within each vessel. The system also allows the organ to be segmented to focus on areas of interest, or to separate venous and arterial blood flow for separate study.

"Beyond its technological capabilities, this new generation of ultrasound technology could lead to significant advances in research and medicine. In the case of hypertensive nephrosclerosis in particular, our device could help us not only better understand the condition but also, likely, identify early biomarkers to improve diagnosis," explains Hannah Plath, a doctoral student at the Institute of Physics for Medicine (Inserm/ESPCI Paris-PSL/CNRS) and the study's first author.

This new generation of ultrasound could well contribute to our understanding of other types of diseases, since, in principle, all organs can be observed in their entirety and with their full vascular complexity.

In a clinical trial, the team will monitor blood flow in the kidneys, as well as in the brain and heart, of patients with atherosclerosis who are candidates for complex surgery.

"This surgical procedure alters blood flow and can compromise these organs. The clinical study aims to predict potential risks for patients," explains Papadacci, who led the research.

How does ultra-high-definition ultrasound imaging of an entire organ work?

To visualize an entire organ with high precision, researchers have developed an ultrasound probe that is much larger than a conventional probe and incorporates numerous components. Acoustic lenses, in particular, are responsible for focusing sound waves with great precision. This probe makes it possible to explore a large volume in three dimensions with high resolution thanks to very high-speed image acquisition.

Finally, microbubbles injected into the bloodstream and carried along by blood flow reveal even the smallest vessels. The combination of these innovations thus makes it possible to achieve two capabilities that were previously difficult to combine: viewing an entire organ and distinguishing its microvasculature.

More information

Hannah Plath et al., Whole-organ mapping of renal microcirculatory haemodynamics in vivo using three-dimensional ultrasound localisation microscopy: a first-in-human feasibility study, The Lancet Medical Imaging & Theranostics (2026). DOI: 10.1016/j.lanmit.2026.100039

item.title: A new map reveals how individual brain cells use different RNA versions of the same genes
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, clear detail

A new map reveals how individual brain cells use different RNA versions of the same genes

In complex organisms such as humans, the same gene can produce different RNA molecules. This is known as alternative splicing. The differently spliced RNA molecules, called isoforms, may in turn result in different proteins.

Not all changes in isoforms have a visible effect. Sometimes, however, the wrong version can have drastic consequences. Incorrect isoforms have been associated with several brain diseases, including ALS, frontotemporal dementia and Alzheimer's disease.

"In these diseases, a protein named TDP-43 leaves its normal place in the cell and forms clumps, so it can no longer do its job," says Andrey Prjibelski, a university researcher at the Department of Computer Science, University of Helsinki.

"As a result, certain RNAs are spliced incorrectly, and neuronal cells lose proteins they need."

Detecting faulty splicing in the brain is not easy. Researchers at the University of Helsinki have now developed a method that maps which gene isoforms the cells in brain tissue use. In the future, it can also be used to identify faulty splicing.

For this work, the team engineered new laboratory techniques as well as algorithms, software and statistical tools for analyzing the data.

Resolution down to single cells

The main goal of the study was to show that spatial isoform mapping at single-cell resolution is possible. This was achieved: the method works at a resolution of 500 nanometers, which is clearly smaller than a single cell. The method was applied to brain samples from mice. The research is published in the journal Nature Methods.

Once the method is applied to samples from people with brain disorders, it may reveal new cases of malfunctioning splicing in specific cells or brain regions. It can also help in studying processes in the healthy brain, such as development, many of which remain understudied.

Toward new drugs that correct splicing

In the long run, these findings may help in designing new drugs for splicing therapy.

For example, since 2016, patients with spinal muscular atrophy, a disease of nerve cells, have been treated with a drug called nusinersen. It works by correcting how the RNA of a gene is processed inside cells. Drugs based on similar principles are now being tested in clinical trials for ALS and dementia.

"Although it's a pretty long way from discovering irregular splicing patterns to new drug candidates for disease treatment, all big things start with smaller steps," Prjibelski says.

Next project: Alzheimer's disease

The next step is to launch projects that analyze human data to study neurological diseases, in particular Alzheimer's disease. The researchers also plan to reanalyze public sequencing archives, which contain large amounts of data that have not been used to their full potential.

"Reanalyzing public data may also yield interesting results without requiring additional resources for sequencing," he says.

Publication details

Lieke Michielsen et al., Spatial isoform sequencing at single-cell resolution reveals cell-type-specific spatial isoform variability in multiple brain cell types, Nature Methods (2026). DOI: 10.1038/s41592-026-03211-w

Journal information: Nature Methods

item.title: Scientists identify brain circuit behind sensory hypersensitivity in autism
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, clear detail

Scientists identify brain circuit behind sensory hypersensitivity in autism

For many people with autism spectrum disorder (ASD), ordinary sensory experiences can be unusually intense or overwhelming. A light touch or a mildly uncomfortable sensation may provoke a disproportionately strong response, making everyday activities difficult.

Sensory abnormalities affect more than 90% of individuals with autism, yet the neural mechanisms underlying these heightened responses remain poorly understood. Scientists have now identified a brain circuit involved in sensory hypersensitivity associated with an autism-related genetic mutation, demonstrating that selectively suppressing specific neurons can alleviate abnormal sensory responses in mice.

A joint research team led by Director Kim Eunjoon of the Center for Synaptic Brain Dysfunctions within the Institute for Basic Science (IBS) and Professor Chung Changuk of KAIST's Graduate School of Medical Science and Engineering has identified excessive neuronal activity in the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) as an important contributor to sensory hypersensitivity in a mouse model of an autism-related disorder. The study is published in the journal Molecular Psychiatry.

The researchers also demonstrate that selectively suppressing certain neurons within this region could alleviate heightened sensory responses, suggesting a potential direction for developing more targeted treatments.

Tracing hypersensitivity to brain circuits

The researchers focused on ADNP (activity-dependent neuroprotective protein), a protein involved in brain development and the regulation of gene expression. Mutations in the ADNP gene cause ADNP syndrome, a rare neurodevelopmental disorder associated with autism and heightened sensitivity to touch and pain. To investigate the underlying mechanisms, the team studied mice lacking one of their two functional copies of the Adnp gene. These mice reacted more strongly to mechanical stimuli, heat and electric shocks than normal mice.

However, mice in which Adnp was deleted in the spinal cord and peripheral tissues, but not the forebrain, did not develop the same abnormalities, suggesting that brain circuits play a major role in the hypersensitivity.

Using neuronal activity mapping and ultrahigh-field functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), the researchers identified excessive activity across several brain regions, particularly the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC), which is involved in processing the emotional aspects of pain.

Further experiments revealed that excitatory neurons in specific layers of the ACC were unusually easy to activate and exhibited altered communication with neighboring cells. These findings suggest that excessive neuronal activity in the ACC could contribute to the heightened sensory responses.

Selective suppression produces different results

To test this possibility, the team used chemogenetics, a technique that allows researchers to control neuronal activity using chemical compounds. Broadly suppressing excitatory neurons in the ACC reduced hypersensitivity to touch and heat but unexpectedly increased freezing behavior during electric shocks.

The researchers then took a more selective approach, inhibiting only ACC neurons that had previously been activated by electric shocks. This intervention normalized the mice's heightened responses to mechanical stimulation and paw heat while also reducing certain shock-related defensive responses.

The contrasting outcomes suggest that targeting specific neuronal populations may be more effective than broadly suppressing activity across an entire brain region, although further studies are needed to determine precisely why the two approaches produced different effects.

Molecular clues point toward targeted treatments

The team also investigated the molecular changes underlying the abnormal neuronal activity. By analyzing gene expression and protein regulation, they identified alterations in pathways associated with synapses and ion channels, which control communication and electrical signaling between neurons.

These changes were particularly prominent in excitatory neurons in specific layers of the ACC, providing additional clues to how reduced ADNP function may contribute to excessive neuronal activity and sensory hypersensitivity.

Kim stated, "Our study demonstrates, at the behavioral, cellular, synaptic and molecular levels, that the hypersensitivity to touch and pain commonly observed in people with autism is closely associated with excessive activity in specific populations of brain neurons, particularly in the anterior cingulate cortex."

He added, "Rather than suppressing activity across an entire brain region, precisely targeting the neuronal populations responsible for these abnormalities may provide an important direction for developing future treatments for sensory hypersensitivity associated with autism."

The findings highlight the importance of higher brain circuits in autism-related sensory abnormalities, extending previous research that has largely emphasized peripheral sensory pathways.

Publication details

Heera Moon et al., ACC hyperactivity and synaptic remodeling underlie sensory hypersensitivity in Adnp-haploinsufficient mice, Molecular Psychiatry (2026). DOI: 10.1038/s41380-026-03972-y

Journal information: Molecular Psychiatry

item.title: PROLIFIC risk score made publicly available to pulmonary fibrosis researchers
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, clear detail

PROLIFIC risk score made publicly available to pulmonary fibrosis researchers

The Pulmonary Fibrosis Foundation and Prognostic Lung Fibrosis Consortium (PROLIFIC) have published a paper in The Lancet Respiratory Medicine detailing the development and validation of the PROLIFIC Risk Score, a novel blood biomarker-based tool designed to predict disease progression in people with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF).

For the first time, the publication makes the methodology and formula behind the PROLIFIC Risk Score publicly available, giving researchers the tools to apply and evaluate the score in their own IPF research. IPF is a life-threatening, progressive disease that causes scarring of the lungs and makes it increasingly difficult to breathe. More than 250,000 Americans are living with IPF and other interstitial lung diseases (ILD), underscoring the urgent need for better treatments.

"Publication of this study in The Lancet Respiratory Medicine is a major milestone for PROLIFIC and for the broader ILD research community," said Peter Schafer, Ph.D., lead author of the study and chair of PROLIFIC. "By publishing the full methodology and formula, researchers can begin evaluating and using the score in their own work while we continue advancing it through the FDA qualification pathway."

Researchers evaluated 12 blood biomarkers reflecting three key processes involved in IPF: lung cell injury, scarring and inflammation. The resulting PROLIFIC Risk Score is designed to estimate the likelihood of disease progression, including lung function decline, lung transplantation or death within one year.

The score was derived and validated in two independent IPF cohorts totaling 886 participants, including 657 participants from the Pulmonary Fibrosis Foundation Patient Registry and 229 participants from the ISABELA Phase III clinical trials.

Addressing a major challenge in IPF research

The clinical course of IPF can vary considerably from one patient to another, making it difficult to predict who will progress quickly and who may experience a slower course of disease. That uncertainty also presents challenges in clinical trials, where differences among participants can make it more difficult to evaluate the effects of an investigational treatment.

The PROLIFIC Risk Score was developed primarily as a drug development tool that could help researchers better characterize the prognosis of clinical trial participants and potentially improve the design and efficiency of IPF studies.

The score is currently progressing through the U.S. Food and Drug Administration's Center for Drug Evaluation and Research Biomarker Qualification Program. In 2025, it became the first IPF biomarker accepted into the program, an early step toward potential qualification for use in drug development.

"The PFF Patient Registry was created so that the experiences and contributions of people living with pulmonary fibrosis and interstitial lung disease could accelerate research," said Scott Staszak, president and CEO of the Pulmonary Fibrosis Foundation. "Seeing registry data contribute directly to the development of the PROLIFIC Risk Score demonstrates exactly why participation in research matters."

Expanding beyond IPF

PROLIFIC is also evaluating whether similar biomarker approaches could have value in other forms of interstitial lung disease.

The consortium has analyzed additional samples, including those from the PROFILE study led by investigators at Imperial College London, as it explores the potential application of prognostic biomarkers beyond IPF.

"Our goal is to understand how these biomarkers can be used most effectively to advance research and drug development across pulmonary fibrosis and other interstitial lung diseases," Schafer said.

Publication details

Multi-biomarker risk score for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis based on serum proteins by the Prognostic Lung Fibrosis Consortium (PROLIFIC): a risk score development and validation study, The Lancet Respiratory Medicine (2026). DOI: 10.1016/S2213-2600(26)00297-3

item.title: Plant‑based 'tuna' or pea chips? Focus groups suggest new recipes for local, sustainable protein alternatives
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, clear detail

Plant‑based 'tuna' or pea chips? Focus groups suggest new recipes for local, sustainable protein alternatives

People prefer plant-based products to be local and sustainable, minimally processed and familiar, according to our latest research. This is alongside typical consumer expectations for food products such as taste and value.

Understanding consumer needs for plant-based food is vital for their success, and that's an essential part of building a more sustainable food system that moves away from carbon-intensive meat products.

Introducing new and exciting plant-based alternatives might encourage meat and dairy lovers to substitute some of their animal-based intake. However, many of those alternatives are ultraprocessed, so there are still potential health concerns surrounding such products.

Our project involved working with consumers to create ideas for plant-based food and drink products. As part of Protein-I, a project investigating how to diversify plant protein production and consumption around Ireland and Northern Ireland, we ran five workshops with consumers.

These workshops focused on plant proteins that could be grown for human consumption locally (such as barley, oats, peas, rye and wheat), rather than ones that are typically imported such as soy. Crop trials across research sites and farms had found that varieties of these crops can be grown in sufficient quantities in countries such as Ireland at a quality suitable for human consumption (rather than animal feed).

Following guided group discussions, interesting ideas from our 38 participants included a plant-based tuna alternative called "toona," made from wheat and pea protein, pea and onion chips plus wheat and barley pasta.

Many ideas focused on peas. However, some of the industry and academic experts we interviewed had reservations about peas, as they have a strong taste and color, which can be off-putting to some people. To make them appealing as an ingredient in products, processing would be needed to refine the taste and color, which may lead to products classed as ultraprocessed and concerns associated with this.

After the 38 participants voted for their favorite products and following input from experts, a vegetarian bolognese and flavored protein oat milk came out as favorites.

A follow-on project from our work (Protein-I-2), which has just started, will explore the development of minimally processed products, using local and sustainable crops.

Research shows that familiarity is an important factor in helping uptake of alternative proteins. Unsurprisingly, many of the food product ideas that originated during our research had similarities to existing products. Our participants weren't given limits on the ideas that they could come up with, yet many of them suggested products based on existing foods such as porridge and pasta.

In our research, when asked what sustainability meant to them, participants often mentioned where a product comes from and locality. One said: "How it's like made … what it is or where it comes from, ye know?" Another commented: "If I'm shopping and I see something that's been flown in from Kenya, beans or something, no, I wouldn't buy. I always go for something that's local."

Plant-based provenance

Highlighting the source or origin of plant-based products on labeling may encourage consumer uptake. As part of the Protein-I project, a digital track-and-trace platform was developed to improve food supply chain transparency. This enables consumers to access information on a product's origin, production journey and environmental footprint through a QR code on the product label.

To explore the connection with local familiar foods, Protein-I ran a hands-on bread-making workshop using Irish-grown cereals. Feedback from participants was positive. Many reported feeling a stronger appreciation of Irish-grown cereals and left with an intention to purchase Irish cereal products in the future.

The workshop helped strengthen participants' connection with where their food comes from and raised awareness of the role Irish-grown cereals can play in a more sustainable food system. By tailoring new product launches to consumers' wants, there is a greater chance of acceptance, which should ultimately be better for sustainability and our environment.

item.title: No, eating celery won't make you lose weight. How we fell for the myth of negative calories
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, clear detail

No, eating celery won't make you lose weight. How we fell for the myth of negative calories

Back in my early days as a dietitian, I used to hear about the miracle properties of celery.

The idea was that you used more energy chomping and digesting celery than you got from the calories in celery.

So the very act of eating celery made you lose weight.

It probably sounded plausible as celery is a low-calorie food. One stalk of celery only contains about 4.3 calories (18 kilojoules).

Celery also takes a lot of chewing, which added to its reputation as a "negative-calorie" food.

So is there any truth to all this? And what do bearded dragon lizards have to do with it?

Can some foods really make you lose weight?

Calories (or kilojoules) refer to the amount of energy a certain food provides. Celery is an example of a nonstarchy vegetable. Like other nonstarchy vegetables, such as cucumber and bell pepper, celery contains virtually no fat or protein and very small amounts of carbohydrates.

Losing weight begins to occur when you are in a negative calorie balance—that is, you use more energy during exercise or everyday activity than you eat.

Because eating fewer calories is a way to manage your weight, it is easy to see how low-calorie celery led to the negative-calorie theory.

How much does it cost to chew and digest food?

The total amount of energy your body burns every day is called the total energy expenditure.

That's made up of the:

- resting metabolic rate, or the calories your body uses to keep you alive at rest, while fasting (that is, whenever you're not moving or eating)

- thermic effect of food, or the "cost" of digesting and absorbing nutrients

- cost of physical activity.

Let's focus on one of those that often confuses people—the thermic effect of food. This is not a "fixed calorie cost." So we cannot say eating a stick of celery uses a certain number of calories. Rather, this thermic effect of food is a percentage of the total energy the food provides.

So a higher-calorie meal will cost more to process than a lower-calorie meal. As the thermic effect of food is expressed as a percentage of the total energy the food provides, you never burn more calories than you eat.

The thermic effect of food also accounts for a small part (about 10%) of your total energy expenditure.

Physical activity can account for 15%–50% of the total, depending on how active you are.

But the resting metabolic rate accounts for about 60%–70%. In other words, the very act of keeping you alive—your brain working, your heart pumping, your core temperature stable, for example—is what uses the highest proportion of calories.

What's the evidence?

One group of researchers tested the concept of "negative-calorie" food on the bearded dragon lizard. This isn't as strange as it sounds. This lizard has been used to study digestion as it processes foods in similar ways to mammals.

This research is posted online as a preprint. As far as I can tell, it has yet to be independently verified by other researchers and published in a peer-reviewed journal.

The lizards ate celery meals equal to 5% of their body weight. The researchers then measured the energy used for chewing and digestion as well as the energy lost in their feces and urine.

As expected, the lizards used energy to digest the celery. But they still gained at least 24% of the meals' energy overall.

I have only found one relevant study in humans, based on research presented to a conference in 2012. Researchers measured how many calories women used after eating 100 grams (3.5 ounces) of celery. A large amount of the calories (86%) in celery was used to chew and digest it. But the women did not burn more calories than what was in the celery.

Together, these studies show celery is not a negative-calorie food.

This myth is an example of the illusory truth effect. This is when repeated exposure to claims makes them seem more believable, even when scientific evidence proves otherwise.

Is celery a con, then?

Celery contains vitamins and minerals. Like all vegetables, it contains other nutrients with antioxidant, anticancer, antimicrobial and anti-inflammatory activity. Celery also contains fiber.

An analysis of all trials looking at celery as a food or as a supplement found it may provide some benefits for high blood pressure, blood sugar and cholesterol levels. However, more studies are needed to confirm this.

So, by all means, eat celery (and other low-calorie, nonstarchy vegetables) in place of energy-dense, nonnutritious foods (such as ultraprocessed snacks and drinks) to support a healthy weight.

But eating celery to give you "negative calories" won't help you magically lose weight.
